mis.DIFF: Treating a difference in observed averages as the causal effect
mis.INTEXT: Mixing up internal and external validity
mis.BOTH: Thinking we can see both potential outcomes for one person
mis.LABEL: Confusing what i, 1 and 0 stand for
mis.THREAT: Mixing up two threats to validity
mis.DIR: Getting the direction (sign or over/under-estimate) wrong
mis.WHO: Confusing who is biased (researcher vs participant)

mcq.stem: In Y₁ᵢ, what does the small 1 stand for?

options.t: The treatment condition: the person gets the treatment (X = 1)
options.why: The 1 says which world we are imagining: treated. Y₀ᵢ is the untreated world.

options.t: The first student in the study
options.why: That is what i does (which unit), and it is not an order. The 1 is about treatment, not position.
Nothing here is about time. The 1 means treated, the 0 means not treated.

options.t: A score of 1 on the outcome
options.why: The 1 is a label for the world, not a value of the outcome.

mcq.stem: In Y₁ᵢ, what does the small i tell us?

options.t: Which unit (person) we are talking about
options.why: i is a name tag: Yᵢ belongs to one specific unit.
That is the 1 or 0. i just says whose outcome it is.

options.t: That it is an average across everyone
options.why: An average would have no i, because it no longer belongs to one unit.
Observed or not is a separate question. i only names the unit.

mcq.stem: A pupil joins a gardening club (Xᵢ = 1) and gets a wellbeing score of 8. Which symbol does the 8 match?

options.t: Y₁ᵢ: the outcome with the club, which is also what we observe
options.why: She is in the club, so the world we see is the treated one: the observed outcome equals Y₁ᵢ.
Y₀ᵢ is her outcome without the club, which we never see for her.
Xᵢ is whether she joined (1 or 0), not a score.
That is her individual causal effect, and needs both outcomes.

mcq.stem: Which best describes a potential outcome?

options.t: What a unit would have with treatment, or without it
options.why: Potential outcomes: Y₁ᵢ (with) and Y₀ᵢ (without). Both exist in principle, only one happens.

options.t: The outcome a researcher actually records
options.why: That is the observed outcome. It equals one of the two potential outcomes.

options.t: The average outcome of the treated group
options.why: That is an average of observed outcomes, not one unit’s potential outcome.

options.t: A prediction about the future from past data
options.why: Potential outcomes are about two possible worlds for one unit, not forecasting.

mcq.stem: Priya won a scholarship and her grade was 72. What is her counterfactual?

options.t: The grade she would have got without the scholarship
options.why: Counterfactual = what would have happened under the condition she did not receive.
72 is what happened. The counterfactual is what did not happen.

options.t: The average grade of everyone with a scholarship
options.why: That is a group average, not Priya’s own path not taken.

options.t: The difference between scholarship and no-scholarship students
options.why: That is a comparison of groups. A counterfactual is about the same person.

mcq.stem: Which formula gives an individual causal effect?

options.why: The effect for unit i: the outcome with treatment minus the outcome without.
Right ingredients, wrong order: this gives the effect with the sign flipped.

options.t: Average of treated − average of control
options.why: That is the naive comparison, a group-level quantity.
Adding the two gives nothing useful. The effect is their difference.

mcq.stem: What is the average treatment effect (ATE)?

options.t: The average of Y₁ᵢ − Y₀ᵢ across all units
options.why: Take every unit’s individual effect, then average them.

options.t: The difference between the average treated outcome and the average control outcome we observe
options.why: That is the naive comparison. It can differ from the ATE.

options.t: The effect for the most typical unit
options.why: The ATE is an average across units, not one typical case.

options.t: The average outcome of the treated group
options.why: That is just one group’s average, with no comparison in it.

mcq.stem: What is a “science table”?

options.t: A table showing both potential outcomes for every unit
options.why: Both Y₁ᵢ and Y₀ᵢ for everyone. Researchers never have one.

options.t: A table of the outcomes we actually observe
options.why: That is ordinary data. A science table has the missing outcomes too.

options.t: A table of only the treated units
options.why: It covers all units, treated and untreated, and both outcomes for each.

options.t: A table of the ATE for each group
options.why: It lists potential outcomes per unit, not summary effects.

mcq.stem: Who can have a science table?

options.t: Only an all-knowing “data god”: researchers never have one
options.why: We only see one potential outcome per unit, so the full table is never available in real data.

options.t: Any researcher who collects enough data
options.why: More data never reveals the path not taken for the same unit.

options.t: Any researcher running a randomised trial
options.why: Randomisation helps comparisons, but it still does not show both outcomes for one unit.

options.t: Anyone, if they ask the participants
options.why: Participants cannot report an outcome from a world that did not happen.

mcq.stem: Which description fits internal validity?

options.t: How confident we can be that the study shows X causes Y
options.why: Internal = is the causal claim sound for the people studied?

options.t: How confident we can be that the results carry over to other people, places and times
options.why: That is external validity.

options.t: How many people are in the study
options.why: Sample size is not what internal validity means.

options.t: How accurately the outcome is measured
options.why: Measurement matters, but internal validity is about the causal claim.

mcq.stem: Which description fits external validity?

options.t: How confident we can be that the results carry over to other people, places and times
options.why: External: who is in the study, and what was the setting?

options.t: How confident we can be that the study shows X causes Y
options.why: That is internal validity.

options.t: Whether the treated and control groups were the same size
options.why: Group sizes are not what external validity is about.

options.t: Whether the study found a statistically significant result
options.why: Significance is about chance, not about who the results apply to.

mcq.stem: What is self-selection?

options.t: Units choosing their own treatment for reasons that also affect the outcome
options.why: It is a form of confounding: the choice and the outcome share a cause.

options.t: Researchers choosing who gets the treatment
options.why: Researcher choice is assignment, not self-selection. Self-selection is the units’ own choice.

options.t: Units dropping out of the study
options.why: Dropping out is attrition.

options.t: Treatment spreading to the control group
options.why: That is contamination.

mcq.stem: What is differential attrition?

options.t: Drop-out that differs between the treated and control groups
options.why: It is not just dropping out: it is different drop-out in the two groups.

options.t: Units choosing which group to join
options.why: That is self-selection.

options.t: Participants guessing what the researcher wants
options.why: That is a demand effect.

options.t: The treatment spilling over to the control group
options.why: That is contamination.

mcq.stem: What is contamination (spillovers)?

options.t: The treatment affecting members of the control group
options.why: The control group is no longer a clean “no treatment” world.

options.t: Control members guessing what the researcher hopes to find
options.why: That is a demand effect.

options.t: Researchers treating the two groups differently
options.why: That is experimenter bias.
That is attrition.

mcq.stem: What is experimenter bias?

options.t: Researchers, often unconsciously, treating the treatment and control groups differently
options.why: The bias comes from the researcher’s side.

options.t: Participants picking up what the researcher hopes to find
options.why: That is a demand effect: the bias comes from participants.

options.t: Participants choosing which group to be in
options.why: That is self-selection.

options.t: Scaling up changing the world around a programme
options.why: That is a general equilibrium effect.

mcq.stem: What are demand effects?

options.t: Participants picking up what the researcher hopes to find, and responding to it
options.why: The change in behaviour comes from the participants.

options.t: Researchers treating the two groups differently
options.why: That is experimenter bias: the bias comes from the researcher.
“Demand” here means responding to what the researcher seems to want, not popularity.

options.t: The treatment spreading to the control group
options.why: That is contamination.

mcq.stem: What are general equilibrium effects?

options.t: Changes that occur when scaling up a programme alters the world around it
options.why: A small pilot may not behave like a full roll-out.

options.t: Differences between the treated and control groups
options.why: That is the naive comparison.
That is contamination, within a study. General equilibrium is about scale.

options.t: Effects that are the same for everyone
options.why: Nothing to do with effects being uniform.

mcq.stem: Families choose whether to sign up for a cycle-to-school scheme. Those who sign up already cycle at weekends and are fitter. Which threat is this?

options.why: They chose treatment for a reason that also affects fitness.
Nothing here says the scheme reached control families.
The problem is who signed up, not what participants guessed.
That would be about scaling up, not who opts in.

mcq.stem: In a language-app trial, 15 of 40 learners given the app quit by week 8 (mostly those finding it hard). Only 3 of 40 in the control group quit. Which threat is this?

options.why: Drop-out differs by group: 15 against 3.
Tempting, because people chose to quit, but the issue is different drop-out across groups.
No sign the app reached the control group.
Nothing here is about researchers treating groups differently.

mcq.stem: Year 4 Class A gets chess lessons; Class B is the control. The classes share a playground, and Class B pupils learn moves from Class A. Which threat is this?

options.why: The treatment spilled into the control group.
Nobody is dropping out in this scenario.
The classes did not choose; the problem is spillover.
Pupils are copying moves, not guessing what researchers want.

mcq.stem: Observers rate pupils’ playground behaviour. They know which pupils attend the new breakfast club. Which threat is most worrying?

options.why: Observers who know who is treated may rate them differently without meaning to.
Demand effects come from participants. Here the issue is the observers.
Nothing here about who chose the club.
Nothing here about drop-out.

mcq.stem: Participants in a wellbeing-app study are told it is “designed to lift your mood”. They then report feeling happier. Which threat is most worrying?

options.why: Participants may report what they think the researcher wants to hear.
The issue is participants’ reports, not researchers’ behaviour.
No spillover to the control group here.
Nothing here about who chose to take part in which group.

mcq.stem: A free bus-pass pilot for 200 families raises attendance. A city-wide roll-out then overcrowds the buses and the gains vanish. Which idea explains this?

options.why: Scaling up changed the world (crowded buses) the pilot relied on.
Contamination is within a study. This is about scaling up.
Families in the pilot may or may not have chosen; the gains vanished because of scale.
Nobody dropped out of the story.

mcq.stem: A study of volunteer pupils at one London school finds a programme works. A critic asks if it would work across England. Which validity is the critic worried about?

options.why: Who is in the study, and where, determines whether results carry over.
Internal validity is about whether the causal claim holds for the people studied.
The critic’s question is only about carrying results to other people and places.
Generalising beyond the study is exactly the question of external validity.

mcq.stem: In a study of a community-garden scheme, residents chose whether to join, and joiners were already healthier. A critic says the result may not reflect the scheme’s effect. Which validity is threatened?

options.why: The comparison is unfair for the people studied: a causal claim problem.
The problem is not who the results apply to but whether the comparison identifies the effect.

options.t: Neither: only the sample is small
options.why: The problem is the comparison, not the sample size.
Self-selection is a classic internal validity problem.

mcq.stem: Three households get a heating subsidy. The council wants each household’s effect of the subsidy on its energy bill. Why can it not simply compute this?

options.t: For each household it observes only one potential outcome: with or without the subsidy
options.why: This is the fundamental problem of causal inference.
Sample size is not the issue: even with millions we never see both for one household.

options.t: Energy bills are measured with error
options.why: Measurement error is separate from the missing-outcome problem.
Differences between households do not stop us seeing both outcomes for one household in principle; it is the missing world that does.

mcq.stem: Which of these is a counterfactual?

options.t: A treated nursery child’s test score had she not attended
options.why: The path not taken for the same unit.

options.t: A treated nursery child’s actual test score
options.why: That is what happened.

options.t: The control group’s average test score
options.why: That is another group’s outcome, not this child’s other path.

options.t: The average gap between the two groups
options.why: A group comparison, not one unit’s other path.

mcq.stem: Pupils who opt into a homework app tend to be keener. The naive comparison of app users and non-users shows users score 9 points higher. The true ATE is probably…

options.t: Smaller than 9: the gap includes keenness, not only the app
options.why: Self-selection inflates the naive comparison.
Keen students scoring higher anyway means the gap overstates the app’s effect.
The naive comparison equals the ATE only if the groups would have been alike without the app.
Possibly smaller, but we cannot say it is zero. The gap just may overstate the effect.

mcq.stem: In a trial of a fitness programme, the control participants who are doing worst drop out. The remaining control group is healthier than the full control group would have been. The estimated effect of the programme will be…

options.why: The control average is inflated, so the gap shrinks.
Opposite: a better-looking control group makes the programme look weaker.
Differential attrition changes who is left to compare.

options.t: Exactly right, because the control group is still randomised
options.why: Randomisation at the start does not protect against drop-out afterwards.

mcq.stem: Why can the naive comparison differ from the ATE?

options.t: It compares different people, so the gap may reflect who got treated, not what treatment did
options.why: Treated and control groups can differ even without treatment.
A small sample can add noise, but the systematic reason is the groups differing.

options.t: Because the ATE ignores some units
options.why: The ATE covers all units. It is the naive comparison that uses only what we observe.
Averages can be compared; the question is whether the groups are alike.

mcq.stem: A study finds a 6-point gap between treated and control. Which conclusion is justified?

options.t: 6 is the naive comparison; it is only the effect if the groups would have been alike without treatment
options.why: The gap equals the effect only under that assumption.

options.t: The treatment raised everyone’s outcome by 6
options.why: A group gap is not an individual effect, and effects can vary.
Causal language needs the groups to be comparable.

options.t: Nothing at all can be concluded
options.why: We can conclude something: that it is a naive comparison, and what would make it causal.

mcq.stem: Which statement about Zoe and a free-bus-pass scheme shows the fundamental problem of causal inference?

options.t: Zoe got the pass, so we see Y₁ᵢ but never Y₀ᵢ
options.why: We observe one potential outcome per person.
That is about who is in the study, i.e. external validity.

options.t: Zoe may have guessed the study’s aim
options.why: That is a demand effect, a different problem.

options.t: Zoe dropped out of the study
options.why: That is attrition, a different problem.

mcq.stem: Which of these is a concern about EXTERNAL validity?

options.t: “The trial only included schools that volunteered, in one city”
options.why: Who is in the study and where: carrying results elsewhere.

options.t: “Pupils chose which group they were in”
options.why: Self-selection: an internal validity concern.

options.t: “Many control pupils learned about the programme from friends”
options.why: Contamination: an internal validity concern.

options.t: “More weaker pupils left the treatment group”
options.why: Differential attrition: an internal validity concern.

mcq.stem: A tutoring programme works well in a pilot with 50 trained tutors. Why might a national roll-out with 5,000 tutors disappoint?

options.t: Scaling up needs many more tutors, who may be less experienced: a general equilibrium effect
options.why: The world changes when the programme scales up.
Possible in any study, but it does not explain why scaling up changes things.
Possible, but the question asks about scaling up.
Possible, but the scale change is the point here.

mcq.stem: A council gives free gym vouchers to half the staff in an office, then compares fitness at the end of the year. Staff with vouchers often invite their deskmates (who have no voucher) to come along. The estimated impact of the vouchers will likely be:

options.t: Too small, because some staff without vouchers also end up exercising
options.why: Yes: the control group is partly treated, so the gap between the groups shrinks.

options.t: Too large, because many staff end up exercising
options.why: Sharing the benefit raises the control group too, which narrows the gap rather than widening it.

options.t: Unaffected, because the deskmates never received a voucher
options.why: They did not receive a voucher, but they still got the treatment second-hand. That leak is exactly what contamination means.

options.t: Reversed in sign, because the vouchers make people exercise less
options.why: Sharing can dilute the effect, but it cannot flip it.

mcq.stem: In a trial of an online maths tool, a few pupils leave the study from both the treated and the control group, at about the same rate. The pupils who leave are no different on average from those who stay. The estimated impact will likely be:

options.t: Unaffected by the attrition, because the same kind of pupil leaves from both groups
options.why: Yes: attrition only biases the estimate when it differs across groups and is linked to the outcome. Neither is true here.

options.t: Too large, because the pupils who leave are the weaker ones
options.why: We are told the leavers are no different from the stayers, so nobody weaker is being lost.

options.t: Too small, because some pupils are lost from the study
options.why: Losing people makes the estimate less precise, but it does not push it in one direction unless who leaves is related to the outcome and differs by group.

options.t: Reversed in sign, because fewer pupils are left in the study
options.why: A smaller sample is noisier, not systematically pointing the wrong way.

mcq.stem: Pupils are randomly assigned to a new reading programme or to normal lessons. Almost everyone completes the study, and treated and control pupils never share materials. The estimated impact will likely be:

options.t: About right on average, because random assignment makes the two groups alike
options.why: Yes: with random assignment, no attrition and no spillovers, the comparison is fair, so a gap points to the programme.

options.t: Too large, because the researchers chose who got the programme
options.why: Researchers using a lottery are not choosing the keen or able pupils, so choice cannot line up with the outcome.

options.t: Too small, because some pupils would have improved anyway
options.why: Pupils improving anyway happens in both groups, so it cancels out when you compare them.

options.t: Reversed in sign, because pupils in normal lessons catch up
options.why: Nothing here pushes the control group up, and chance alone would not systematically flip the sign.

mcq.stem: Patients choose between a specialist hospital and their local clinic. The sickest patients tend to choose the hospital, and they are so much sicker that their recovery rate ends up lower than the clinic's, even though the hospital really does help each patient. Reading that gap as the impact of the hospital, the estimate will likely be:

options.t: Reversed in sign, because the hospital's patients were much sicker to begin with
options.why: Yes: the hospital group started far worse off. Here that head start outweighs the real benefit, so the naive gap makes a helpful hospital look harmful.

options.t: Too large, because the patients who choose the hospital benefit most
options.why: The sickest patients choosing the hospital makes it look worse, not better.

options.t: Too small but still positive, because the hospital group is sicker
options.why: Too small is the right direction, but in this case the gap is negative, so it is not just understated, it points the wrong way.

options.t: Unaffected, because both groups of patients got some treatment
options.why: Choosing your own treatment is exactly what lets the groups differ. Here that difference drives the whole gap.

short.q: A study of a reading app is run only in volunteer schools. Pupils within each school were randomly assigned to use the app or not. Say what the study does well and what it does less well.
model: Internal validity is strong: random assignment makes the groups alike, so a gap points to the app.
External validity is weaker: volunteer schools may differ from other schools.
Link: a fair comparison does not mean the result carries over.

short.q: Pupils chose whether to join a lunchtime science club. Club members scored 8 points higher in science. Does this show the club raised scores?
model: No, not by itself: 8 is a naive comparison.
Members chose the club, so they may already be keener or stronger: self-selection.
It would only be the effect if the groups would have scored the same without the club.

short.q: Mia is offered after-school tutoring and takes it. Her end-of-term maths score is 64. Why can we never calculate Mia’s individual causal effect of the tutoring directly?
model: Mia either has tutoring or does not, so we see only one potential outcome.
Her individual effect is Y₁ᵢ − Y₀ᵢ and needs both.
This is the fundamental problem of causal inference.

short.q: In a trial, 30% of treated participants but 5% of controls dropped out. Name the threat and say how it could bias the estimate.
model: Differential attrition: drop-out differs between groups.
If those leaving the treated group were the weaker ones, the remaining treated group looks better.
So the estimated effect could be too large.

short.q: A pilot of free breakfasts raised attendance. Why might a national roll-out give a different result?
model: General equilibrium effects: scaling up changes the setting around the programme.
For example, demand for food, staff or space changes, so the pilot’s conditions no longer hold.
The pilot result may not carry over, an external validity concern.

short.q: Markers know which pupils took a revision workshop and pupils know the workshop is meant to raise grades. Name two threats and say who each comes from.
model: Experimenter bias: the markers might grade workshop pupils more generously.
Demand effects: pupils might try harder or report more effort because they guess the aim.
The first comes from researchers, the second from participants.

labels.fund: The fundamental problem of causal inference

caps.selfsel: people choosing their own group for reasons that also affect the outcome
caps.attrit: more people leaving one group than the other
caps.contam: the treatment leaking into the control group
caps.expbias: the researcher treating or judging the groups differently
caps.demand: participants guessing what the researcher wants and responding to it
caps.ge: a programme changing the world around it when it scales up
caps.fund: only ever seeing one of a person’s two possible outcomes
caps.indiv: the gap between one person’s two potential outcomes
caps.internal: groups that are alike, so a gap is down to the treatment
caps.external: results from one sample being carried to a wider population
caps.counter: what would have happened on the path not taken
caps.naive: comparing the averages of two different groups

tips.DIFF: A difference between group averages is not automatically an effect. It only equals the effect if the groups would have been alike without treatment.
tips.INTEXT: Internal = is the comparison fair for the people studied? External = would it carry over to other people, places and times?
tips.THREAT: Match each threat to who or what causes it: self-selection = people choose; attrition = people leave unequally; contamination = treatment leaks; experimenter bias = researchers; demand = participants.
tips.DIR: To get direction right: ask which group ends up looking better or worse because of the problem, then whether that widens or shrinks the gap.
tips.BOTH: We only ever see one of a person’s two potential outcomes. The other is the counterfactual.
tips.LABEL: Y is the outcome, the small 1 or 0 says treated or not, and i says which person.
tips.WHO: Experimenter bias comes from the researchers. Demand effects come from the participants.
tips.DEF: Re-read the glossary wording for the two terms you swapped.
tips.CALC: Write each step: first the two averages, then subtract. Check you divided.

gloss: How confident we can be that a study establishes that X causes Y. Common problems include self-selection into treatment, differential attrition, experimenter bias.
How confident we can be that a study’s results carry over to other people, places and times. Think: who is in the study, and what was the setting?
The outcomes a unit would have with treatment (Y₁ᵢ) and without it (Y₀ᵢ).
What would have happened to the same unit under the treatment condition it did not receive.
The difference between a unit’s two potential outcomes: Y₁ᵢ − Y₀ᵢ.
We can never observe both potential outcomes for the same unit.
The average of Y₁ᵢ − Y₀ᵢ across all units in a group.
Units choosing their own treatment for reasons that also affect Y. It is a form of confounding.
A table showing both potential outcomes for every unit. Researchers never have one; an all-knowing data god does.
The difference in average observed outcomes between treated and control units. It can differ from the ATE because of self-selection.
Drop-out that differs between the treated and control groups.
The treatment affecting members of the control group.
Researchers, often unconsciously, treating the treatment and control groups differently.
Participants picking up what the researcher hopes to find, and responding to it.
Changes that occur when scaling up a programme alters the world around it.
